summary: No factual errors were found in the 180 questions; read-code explanations were hand-traced and agree with the verified outputs, so rejection was about relative quality. Selected questions were mostly realistic bug scenarios (shallow-copy config, except ordering, join fan-out, NOT IN with NULL, LRU cache, top-k heap) where a candidate holding a listed misconception gives a recognisably different answer. Rejected questions were usually near-duplicates of a stronger one (e.g. the repeated AND/OR precedence and DISTINCT items in SQL L1, multiple GIL or class-attribute questions in Python L3), thin or textbook (simple stack traces, ACID definitions), dense or trick-like (PY-L3-103), or a poor fit for their level (SQL-L3-103 and SQL-L3-120 are L2 content). The coverage rules forced some trade-offs. Misconceptions that appear only in a few questions forced pairs that overlap in theme: PY-L3-102 with PY-L3-119 (class attributes), SQL-L3-108 with SQL-L3-119 (NOT IN with NULL), and DS-L3-107 with DS-L3-108 plus DS-L3-112 with DS-L3-117 (graph traversal). Some good questions also had to give way to questions that carry needed misconceptions, e.g. DS-L1-101 to DS-L1-108 and PY-L2-117 to PY-L2-109. The set was chosen by a constrained search that maximises total score minus a near-duplicate penalty, and no single or double swap improves it.
